citations.quote: A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

derivations.claim: For each finite $N$, orthonormality [F2] gives $\|f_N\|_H^2=\sum_{0\le l\le N}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\xi_{lk}^2.$ The nonnegative partial sums increase to the full coefficient-square sum, so [F4] gives its expectation as the limit of the finite expectations, $\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\mathbb E\xi_{lk}^2=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^l2^{-2l(\alpha+1/2)}=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty,$ since the final series is geometric with ratio $2^{-2\alpha}<1$. If the coefficient-square sum were infinite on an event of probability $p>0$, its expectation would be at least $Rp$ for every $R>0$, contradicting finiteness. Thus that sum is finite almost surely.

On the probability-one event where that sum is finite, for $M>N$ orthonormality gives $\|f_M-f_N\|_H^2=\sum_{N<l\le M}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\xi_{lk}^2.$ The right side tends to zero uniformly over $M>N$ as $N\to\infty$, since it is a tail of a convergent nonnegative series. Thus $(f_N)$ is Cauchy in $H$ and has a limit $f$ by completeness [F1]. When $H=L^2([0,1])$, completeness is supplied by [F5] under [A1]. The Cauchy event is measurable because it is a countable combination of conditions on the measurable distances $\|f_M-f_N\|_H$. On that event the pointwise limit is measurable as a limit into the separable metric space $H$; setting the limit equal to zero on the measurable complement gives a Borel $H$-valued random element.

The same monotone-convergence calculation in [F4] gives $\mathbb E\|f\|_H^2=\mathbb E\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\xi_{lk}^2=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty.$ This proves both the stated second-moment formula and the claimed well-definedness.

citations.quote: For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

derivations.claim: Assume $\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$, and fix a nonempty closed set $F\subseteq S$. For every integer $m\ge1$, the function $g_m(x)=(1-md(x,F))_+$ satisfies $0\le g_m\le1$ and $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g_m)\le m$. Hence $g_m/m$ is admissible in the definition of $\beta_{BL}$, so $\int g_m\,d\mu_n\to\int g_m\,d\mu$. Since $1_F\le g_m$, it follows that $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\int g_m\,d\mu$ for every $m$.

Now assume $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$, and put $\mathcal A=\{\mu\}\cup\{\mu_n:n\ge1\}$. Any sequence chosen from $\mathcal A$ either has a member repeated infinitely often, yielding a constant convergent subsequence, or has a subsequence of the form $(\mu_{n_j})$ with $n_j\to\infty$, which converges weakly to $\mu$. Therefore $\mathcal A$ is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

The functions $g_m$ decrease pointwise to $1_F$ and are bounded by the integrable constant function $1$ under the probability $\mu$. By [F4], $\int g_m\,d\mu\to\mu(F)$, so the closed-set bound holds; it is trivial for $F=\varnothing$. The Portmanteau theorem [F2] gives weak convergence in the sense of [F1].

By [F5], $S$ is Polish; therefore [F3] applies under [A1] and $\mathcal A$ is tight. Thus for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq S$ such that $\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal A}\nu(K^c)<\varepsilon$.

Fix $\eta>0$. Compactness gives a finite $\eta/8$-net $x_1,\dots,x_q$ of $K$. Quantize each value $g(x_i)\in[-1,1]$ into finitely many bins of width at most $\eta/2$. There are finitely many resulting value patterns for the bounded 1-Lipschitz test class; choose one representative $h_r$ from each nonempty pattern. If $g$ and $h_r$ share a pattern, then for $x\in K$ a net point $x_i$ gives $|g(x)-h_r(x)|\le2d(x,x_i)+|g(x_i)-h_r(x_i)|<\eta$.

For any admissible $g$, choose the representative $h_r$ from its pattern. The integral difference is bounded by $\left|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g\,d\mu\right|\le\max_r\left|\int h_r\,d\mu_n-\int h_r\,d\mu\right|+2\eta+2\mu_n(K^c)+2\mu(K^c).$ The maximum tends to zero by [F1], because there are finitely many bounded continuous representatives, and the last two terms are at most $4\varepsilon$ by step 2.2. Taking the supremum over $g$, then the limit superior in $n$, gives $\limsup_n\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\le2\eta+4\varepsilon$. Letting $\eta,\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the reverse implication.

derivations.claim: Write $w_l=a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$. In the wavelet case, the trace sum is a finite coarsest term plus $\sum_{l\ge1}2^lw_l=(\log2)^{-2\delta}\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$. On each block $2^m\le l<2^{m+1}$, the sum of $l^{-r}$ is between $2^m2^{-r(m+1)}$ and $2^m2^{-rm}$; hence $\sum_m m^{-r}$ converges exactly when $r>1$, by the same block comparison. For trigonometric coefficients with bounded multiplicities, the block $2^m\le |l|<2^{m+1}$ contributes between constant multiples of $m^{-2\delta}$ to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The same comparison therefore gives finiteness exactly when $\delta>1/2$. Thus the trace $T_\delta:=\sum_{l,k}w_l$ is finite in either case.

Let $S_m$ be the sum of $w_lZ_{lk}^2$ over the first $m$ coordinates in the fixed countable enumeration. These nonnegative partial sums increase to $S=\sum_{l,k}w_lZ_{lk}^2$, and [F3] gives $\mathbb ES=\lim_m\mathbb ES_m=\sum_{l,k}w_l=T_\delta$. Integration by parts in the displayed normal density gives $\mathbb EZ_{lk}^2=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int x^2e^{-x^2/2}dx=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-x^2/2}dx=1$. If $S=\infty$ on a set of probability $p>0$, then $\mathbb ES\ge Rp$ for every $R>0$, impossible; hence $S<\infty$ almost surely.

On that probability-one event, the finite-coordinate sums of $W$ are Cauchy in $H(\delta)$ because the squared norm of every tail is the corresponding tail of the convergent series $S$. Completeness gives a limit in $H(\delta)$. The Cauchy event is measurable, and the partial sums are measurable; their pointwise limit on that event is measurable as an $H(\delta)$-valued map because the space is separable. Setting it to zero on the measurable complement gives a Borel random element.

Let $e_j$ be the unit vector of the weighted sequence Hilbert space supported on coordinate $j$ and let $b_j=L(e_j)$ for a continuous real linear functional $L$. For each finite set $F$, boundedness applied to $\sum_{j\in F}b_je_j$ gives $\sum_{j\in F}b_j^2\le\|L\|^2$, so $\sum_jb_j^2<\infty$. The finite-coordinate projections of $W$ converge in $H(\delta)$ by step 3.1, hence continuity gives $L(W)=\lim_F\sum_{j\in F}\sqrt{w_j}b_jZ_j$. The finite sums are centered normal with variances $v_F=\sum_{j\in F}w_jb_j^2$, and $v_F\to v:=\sum_jw_jb_j^2<\infty$. Their tails have second moment equal to the corresponding variance tail, so the sums converge to $L(W)$ in $L^2$. Since $|e^{itx}-e^{ity}|\le |t||x-y|$, their characteristic functions converge to that of $L(W)$; the limit is $e^{-t^2v/2}$. Thus every continuous linear functional of $W$ is Gaussian.

Enumerate the infinite basis as $(\psi_j)_{j\ge1}$, write its white-noise coordinates as $Z_j$, and let $A_j=\{|Z_j|\ge1\}$. The displayed normal density is positive on $[1,2]$, so $p:=\mathbb P(A_j)>0$; independence gives $\mathbb P(\bigcap_{j=m}^{m+q}A_j^c)=(1-p)^{q+1}$. By [F4], $\mathbb P(\bigcap_{j\ge m}A_j^c)=0$ for each $m$, so the event that only finitely many $A_j$ occur, a countable union of these intersections, has probability zero. Therefore $\sum_{j\le n}Z_j^2$ is unbounded almost surely. If the same $H(\delta)$ element were represented by an $L^2$ function, the coefficient embedding in [F1] would identify its $L^2$ coefficients with $Z_j$. The finite Pythagorean identity, applied to the projection onto $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_n$, would then give $\sum_{j\le n}Z_j^2\le\|W\|_2^2$ for every $n$, a contradiction.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate $j$, the pair $(\theta_j,X_j)$ is a measurable function of the independent pair $(\xi_j,Z_j)$. Thus the coordinate pairs are independent: finite rectangle probabilities factor by [F1] and [F2]. Fix finite $J$. For any cylinder event $B$ depending on finitely many observations outside $J$, the random vector $(\theta_J,X_J)$ is independent of $B$ by that same factorization. The events in $\sigma(X_{J^c})$ for which this independence identity holds form a lambda-system containing the outside-coordinate cylinder pi-system; [F3] extends it to all outside-data events. Hence conditioning on $X_{J^c}$ adds no information about $\theta_J$ once $X_J$ is known.

For finite $J$, the joint prior density of $\theta_J$ is the product of $\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t_j/\sigma_j)$, and the likelihood of $X_J=x_J$ is proportional to $\prod_{j\in J}e^{-n(x_j-t_j)^2/2}$. Each one-dimensional normalizer is at most $1$ and is positive: the Gaussian factor is bounded by $1$, is strictly positive everywhere, and the prior density integrates to $1$. Thus the normalized product density is $\prod_{j\in J}p_{j,n}(t_j\mid x_j)$. Integrating it over rectangles in $\theta_J$ and $X_J$ verifies the conditional-law identity for these coordinates. The prior is a Borel probability on $L^2$ by [L1] under [A1], and [A2] supplies the full posterior kernel; step 1.1 extends the finite-coordinate identity to the full observation sequence.

The product of the one-coordinate conditional densities in step 2.1 is exactly the stated finite-dimensional posterior marginal, so the posterior factors by coordinates for every finite index set $J$.

For $\delta>1/2$ the contribution is proportional to $l^{-2\delta}$; on each dyadic block its sum is at most a constant times $2^{m(1-2\delta)}$, a summable geometric sequence. Finite coarsest terms do not affect either conclusion.
By [F2] the coefficient sequence defines a Borel Gaussian law on $H(\delta)$ and is not $L^2$-valued; [F3] gives tightness of that law under [A1].

Therefore the canonical Gaussian target for the weak BvM result is the negative-Sobolev law described in [F2], tight under the stated AC branch [F3]; the theorem makes no $L^2$-valued or total-variation conclusion.

derivations.claim: The normal density is bounded and continuous, is bounded below by $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-2}$ on $(-2,2)$, and has finite second moment $1$. The normalized truth coefficients all equal $r_{lk}=1$, hence $\sup_{l,k}|r_{lk}|=1\le M=1<\tau=2$.

The deterministic truth series is in $L^2$ because orthogonality gives $\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{k\in K_l}\theta_{0,lk}^2=\sum_{l\ge0}2^l\sigma_l^2=\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty$. The prior is likewise $L^2$-valued by [F1] under [A1].

All hypotheses of [F2] now hold, including continuity at each $r_{lk}=1$; therefore for every $\delta>1/2$ the scaled posterior converges to canonical white noise in the bounded-Lipschitz metric of $H(\delta)$.
